pages.title: Embedded queries and saved searches
pages.description: A ```query block lists the notes that match a search, a ```dataview block runs common Obsidian Dataview queries, and saved searches sit in the sidebar. All of them update as the vault changes.
pages.md:
## ```query blocks

Write a search in a `query` block and the preview lists the notes that
match it, kept up to date as you save notes:

````markdown
```query
tag:project -tag:done
view: table
sort: modified desc
limit: 20
```
````

The search uses the same [operators](/workspace/search-operators/) as the
search dialog: words, `tag:`, `path:`, `"exact phrase"`, `/regex/` and
`-term` to leave notes out. Lines of the form `option: value` set how it
shows:

| Option | Values | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `view` | `list`, `table` (note, folder, modified, tags) | `list` |
| `sort` | `relevance`, `name`, `path`, `modified` — then `asc` or `desc` | `relevance` |
| `limit` | 1–500 | 50 |

A line starting with `//` is a comment. The note that holds the block is
never in its own results. An option it can't read is shown above the
results, not silently dropped.

## ```dataview blocks

Vaults that come from Obsidian are full of
[Dataview](https://blacksmithgu.github.io/obsidian-dataview/) blocks.
Lumen runs the common part of its query language, so they render here
without the plugin:

````markdown
```dataview
TABLE status, due FROM #project WHERE status != "done" SORT due ASC
```
````

- **`LIST [expr]`** and **`TABLE [WITHOUT ID] expr [AS "name"], …`**
- **`FROM`** `#tag`, `"folder"`, `[[note]]` (notes that link to it), with
  `AND`, `OR`, `-` and parentheses
- **`WHERE`** comparisons (`= != < > <= >=`), `and` / `or` / `!`, `+ - * /`
- **`SORT`** one or more fields, `ASC` / `DESC`; **`LIMIT`** n
- Fields: front matter, inline fields (`key:: value`, `[key:: value]`) and
  `file.name`, `file.path`, `file.folder`, `file.link`, `file.mtime`,
  `file.ctime`, `file.size`, `file.tags`, `file.outlinks`
- Functions: `contains`, `icontains`, `startswith`, `endswith`, `length`,
  `lower`, `upper`, `date(today)`, `dur(7 days)`, `default`, `choice`,
  `round`, `number`, `string`, `join`, `regexmatch`

`TASK`, `CALENDAR`, `GROUP BY`, `FLATTEN` and DataviewJS are not supported:
the block says so instead of guessing. Nothing in a query is run as code —
the language is parsed and interpreted, and a test checks that the query
code has no `eval`.

## Live updates

Both kinds of block re-run when a note is saved, deleted or renamed. In a
vault of 1,000 notes, re-running after a save takes well under 100 ms.

## Saved searches

In the search dialog, **☆ Save search** keeps the search. Saved searches are
listed at the top of the file sidebar; a click opens the dialog on that
search again, and × removes it. They are kept in this browser, not in the
vault.

pages.title: EPUB reader and reading mode
pages.description: Read EPUB books in the vault (Hebrew right-to-left included), highlight them like PDFs, and read clipped pages in a calm reading mode.
pages.md:
Lumen opens EPUB books from your vault in a reader of its own. Your books,
their fonts and pictures stay on the device: nothing is fetched while you
read. A link in a book that leads to a website is shown, not opened.

## Open a book

- **Command palette** (⌘K / Ctrl+K) → **Open an EPUB for reading…** copies a
  book from your computer into the vault and opens it.
- **File tree**: click a `.epub` file.
- **A link** in a note: `[[book.epub]]`, or `[[book.epub#chapter=3]]` to open
  it at chapter 3.

The reader opens at the chapter where you stopped. **Contents** shows the
book's table of contents. The arrow keys go to the previous or next chapter;
in a right-to-left book they follow its direction. Hebrew and Arabic books
are shown right to left, with the book's own fonts.

## Reading settings

**Light**, **Sepia** or **Dark**, **A−** / **A+** for the text size, and
**⇥⇤** / **⇤⇥** for the line width. The settings are kept for each book (and
each note in reading mode) on this device.

## Highlights

Select text and press **Highlight** (or **H**). Highlights work like the
[PDF reader's](/workspace/pdf-reader/): each one is saved as a W3C Web
Annotation in a note next to the book, `book.epub.md`. Each highlight there
is a line with a link such as `[[book.epub#chapter=2&highlight=…]]`, which
opens the book at that chapter and flashes the highlight. Add a note to a
highlight, or remove it, under **Highlights**. Write your own notes anywhere
in `book.epub.md` outside the highlights block; Lumen only changes that
block.

## Reading mode for clipped pages

**Command palette → Reading mode** shows the open note as a page to read,
with the same themes, size and width. It is made for pages clipped from the
web: the source and the date the page was clipped are shown at the top.
Select a passage and press **Highlight** (or **H**). The passage is marked
in the note itself as `==…==`, the web clipper's highlight syntax, so the
highlight lives in the Markdown and syncs with it. A passage across
paragraphs, links or formatting can't be marked. Run the command again, or
press Esc, to leave.

pages.title: Export and import
pages.description: Take the whole vault out as a .zip or a folder, bring in an Obsidian vault or a Notion export, and convert single files to and from many formats.
pages.md:
Your notes are plain Markdown, and they can always leave Lumen.

## The whole vault

**Export:** `⌘K → Export the whole vault…`. Pick a **.zip** download or,
where the browser can write folders (Chrome, Edge), a **folder**. Every note
and attachment is written with its folder path. A folder export goes into
a new `lumen-vault-<date>` subfolder, so nothing already in the folder you
picked is overwritten. The note you are editing is saved first.

**Import:** `⌘K → Import notes from another app (Obsidian, Notion, Evernote, Bear, Keep, Logseq, OneNote…)…`.
Pick a .zip or a folder. Lumen recognises:

| Source | Recognised by | What import does |
|---|---|---|
| Obsidian vault | an `.obsidian/` folder | notes and attachments as they are; `.obsidian/` itself is skipped |
| Notion export | most file names end in Notion's 32-character ID | IDs are removed from the names, and the links between pages are rewritten to the new names |
| Lumen export, or any folder | otherwise | everything as it is |

Everything is imported into a **new folder** (`Imported/<name>`, numbered
when that name is taken), so no existing note is ever overwritten. Two
pages that end up with the same name are numbered (`Page 2.md`).
`.git`, `.trash`, `__MACOSX` and `.DS_Store` are skipped. When the import
finishes, a message says how many notes and files came in and where.

## One document

**Out:** the *File* menu and the palette export the open note to HTML,
Word (.doc), RTF, LaTeX, reStructuredText, AsciiDoc, Org-mode, OPML,
slides (Reveal.js), EPUB, Jupyter (.ipynb), PowerPoint (.pptx), a static
site, and PDF (`⌘K → Print / Save as PDF…`). Right-to-left text keeps its
direction in the exported files.

**In:** open a file (`⌘O`) or drop it on the window. Besides Markdown and
text, Lumen converts HTML, RTF, CSV / TSV, JSON, XML, Word (.docx and the
older .doc), OpenDocument (.odt), PowerPoint (.pptx), Excel (.xlsx),
EPUB, PDF (with OCR for scanned pages), MHTML, OPML, LaTeX,
reStructuredText, AsciiDoc, Org-mode, Jupyter notebooks, Apple Pages /
Numbers / Keynote, Fountain screenplays and .zip archives into a Markdown
note.

## How it is tested

The vault round trip (export, then import), the Obsidian and Notion
detection, Notion's link rewrite and the duplicate-name numbering are unit
tests over `src/storage/exportAll.ts`. Each format converter has its own
tests.

pages.title: Graph and local graph
pages.description: The knowledge graph of the whole vault — 10,000 notes and 50,000 links — and the local graph of the open note, with filters, colour groups and full keyboard use.
pages.md:
## The graph

**Knowledge Graph** (command palette) shows every note of the vault, and a line
for every `[[link]]` between two notes.

- **Big vaults.** The graph is built from the vault index, so the notes
  are not read again. The layout is computed in a background worker; the
  picture appears at once and settles over a second or two. Nodes and
  links are drawn with WebGL, so 10,000 notes and 50,000 links pan and
  zoom smoothly. While you move the view, a sample of the links is drawn;
  all of them come back as soon as you stop.
- **Filters.** Narrow the graph by **tag** (nested tags included:
  `project` keeps `project/active`), by **folder** (and its subfolders),
  or by a frontmatter **property**: `status=open`, or just `status` for any
  note that has one.
- **Colour groups.** Colour the notes by their top folder or their first
  tag. The legend shows the twelve biggest groups.
- **Labels** show for the bigger notes, and for more of them as you zoom
  in. Hebrew names are shaped and written right to left.

## The local graph

**Show / hide the local graph** opens a panel beside the note: the open
note in the middle, and the notes within **1, 2 or 3** links of it. It has
the same tag and folder filters, and is coloured by folder. It follows you
as you open other notes, and opens in well under a fifth of a second.

## With the keyboard

The graph is one focusable area. Tab to it, and:

| Key | Does |
|---|---|
| ← ↑ → ↓ | go to the linked note in that direction (or, if there is none, the nearest note that way) |
| Enter | open the focused note |
| + / − | zoom in / out |
| 0 | fit the whole graph |
| Shift + arrows | pan |
| Home | back to the biggest note (in the local graph: the open note) |

The focused note's name and number of links are announced to screen
readers. In the full graph, the **Find a note** box jumps to any note by
name, so every note can be reached without a mouse.

pages.title: Daily notes and the Hebrew calendar
pages.description: The calendar's holidays, fasts and weekly Torah portion, for Israel or the diaspora, and the {{holiday}} and {{parasha}} placeholders of the daily note.
pages.md:
**Show / hide the calendar** (command palette) shows a month under the file tree. A day with a daily
note is marked; clicking a day opens its note, or creates it from your
template.

## Holidays and the Torah portion

The calendar knows the Jewish year: the festivals, the fasts, Rosh Chodesh,
the Israeli national days, and the Torah portion of every Shabbat.

- Days with a holiday or a fast have a mark on top. Hover a day, or reach
  it with a screen reader, for its civil date, its Hebrew date, its holidays
  and, on Shabbat, its portion.
- Under the grid, the month's holidays are listed by day.
- Names are in Hebrew when the UI is in Hebrew, and in English otherwise.

### Israel or the diaspora

The festivals have one day of yom tov in Israel and two in the diaspora, so
the two calendars differ: Simchat Torah, the eighth day of Pesach and the
second day of Shavuot are diaspora days only. When one of them falls on
Shabbat, Israel reads the next Torah portion that week, and the two
schedules realign a few weeks later, when the diaspora reads two portions
together and Israel reads them separately.

The **⚙ settings** of the calendar have a checkbox,
**Holidays and Torah portions as in Israel**. Until you change it, Lumen
picks Israel when the UI is in Hebrew or your time zone is Israel's.

### What is included

| | |
|---|---|
| Festivals | Rosh Hashana, Yom Kippur, Sukkot with Chol HaMoed and Hoshana Raba, Shemini Atzeret and Simchat Torah, Pesach with Chol HaMoed, Shavuot |
| Fasts | Tzom Gedaliah, 10 Tevet, Ta'anit Esther, Ta'anit Bechorot, 17 Tammuz, Tish'a B'Av |
| Other days | Chanukah, Tu BiShvat, Purim Katan, Purim, Shushan Purim, Pesach Sheni, Lag BaOmer, Tu B'Av, the eve of the festivals, Rosh Chodesh |
| Israeli days | Yom HaShoah, Yom HaZikaron, Yom HaAtzmaut, Yom Yerushalayim |

Fasts that fall on Shabbat move as they do in practice: Tzom Gedaliah,
17 Tammuz and Tish'a B'Av to Sunday, Ta'anit Esther and Ta'anit Bechorot to
Thursday. Yom HaShoah, Yom HaZikaron and Yom HaAtzmaut move as Israeli law
sets them, so that they never touch Shabbat.

## In the daily note

Two placeholders join `{{date}}`, `{{hebrewDate}}`, `{{weekday}}` and
`{{title}}` in the daily-note template:

| Placeholder | Becomes |
|---|---|
| `{{holiday}}` | the day's holidays, separated by `·`, or nothing |
| `{{parasha}}` | this week's Torah portion (the Shabbat on or after the day), or the festival read instead |

For example, the template

```markdown
# {{title}}

{{hebrewDate}} · {{parasha}} {{holiday}}
```

gives, on Friday 16 May 2025 in Israel, a line with the Hebrew date,
`Emor` and `Lag BaOmer` (in a Hebrew UI: `פרשת אמור` and `ל״ג בעומר`).

## How it is computed

The calendar is Lumen's own code: the fixed Hebrew calendar (the molad and
the four postponements of Rosh Hashana), the holiday rules, and the rules
for which Torah portions are read together, from the Shulchan Aruch. No
calendar library is used; the common one is under the GPL, which Lumen
does not ship. A whole year — holidays and every Shabbat, for Israel and
for the diaspora — is computed in a few milliseconds, in your browser.

The tests check the arithmetic against the browser's own Hebrew calendar on
every day from 1990 to 2060, and every holiday rule against a hand-checked
table of the years 2025–2030.


## Your morning

`⌘K` → **Daily note: “Your morning”** adds a block to today's note, and from
then on writes it each morning when you open today's note. It is off until
you run it, and `⌘K` → **Daily note: turn off “Your morning”** stops it.

The block has:

- the Hebrew date, this week's parasha and today's holidays;
- the notes changed since the last morning, newest first (daily notes are
  left out);
- the open tasks due today or earlier. Due dates can be written as
  `📅 2026-11-12` (Tasks), `[due:: 2026-11-12]` (Dataview) or
  `@due(2026-11-12)`;
- how many review cards are waiting, with the first few.

Every row links to its note or card.

Everything comes from this device: the vault index that search keeps in
memory, `.lumen/review.json` and the Hebrew calendar. Nothing is sent
anywhere. On a 10,000-note vault the block takes a few milliseconds, once
the index is built.

The block sits between `<!-- lumen:morning:start -->` and
`<!-- lumen:morning:end -->`. Writing it again replaces only that part, so
your own text in the note stays as it is. While today's note is open with
edits, the block is written into the editor instead of the file.

pages.title: Import highlights (Kindle, Kobo, Readwise, Zotero)
pages.description: Bring your highlights from Kindle, Kobo, Readwise and Zotero into the vault, one note per book, with no duplicates when you import again.
pages.md:
Run `⌘K → "Import highlights (Kindle, Kobo, Readwise, Zotero)…"`, pick
where the highlights come from, then pick the file.

| From | What to pick |
|---|---|
| **Kindle** | `My Clippings.txt` in the Kindle's `documents` folder (connect it by USB). |
| **Kobo** | `KoboReader.sqlite` in the reader's hidden `.kobo` folder. |
| **Readwise** | The CSV export: Readwise → Export → CSV. |
| **Zotero** | Nothing to pick: Zotero 7 on this computer, desktop app only (see below). |

Every book or article gets a note, `Highlights/ — .md`. Each
highlight is a quote with:

- its place (page, location, or chapter and %);
- the date;
- tags and your note;
- for Zotero, a link that opens the annotation in its PDF.

Hebrew titles and texts work, file names included.

## Import again, any time

Importing the same file again only adds what's new:

- A highlight that's already in the note is left as it is, including any
  edits you made to it.
- If the app changed it (for example, you edited its note in Readwise),
  the entry is updated.
- A highlight you extended on the Kindle replaces the shorter one.
- The same passage from two apps (a Kindle highlight that Readwise also
  has) is **one** entry.
- Whatever you write in the note outside the highlights is kept.

Bookmarks, Kobo dog-ears and Zotero image or ink annotations have no text
and are left out; the import says how many.

Imported highlights appear in [All highlights](/workspace/highlights/)
under the kind **Imported**, and can be searched like the rest.

## Zotero

Zotero 7 serves your library to other apps on the same computer.

1. Turn it on in Zotero: **Settings → Advanced → "Allow other applications
   on this computer to communicate with Zotero"**.
2. With Zotero open, run the import in the **desktop app**. It reads your
   annotations from `127.0.0.1` (your own computer) and never from the
   cloud.

Zotero refuses requests from web pages, so in the browser the import
explains this instead.

Nothing is uploaded: the files are read on this device, and the only
request made is the desktop app's request to Zotero on this computer.

pages.title: All highlights
pages.description: Every highlight from PDFs, books and clipped pages in one place: search them, tag them, export them to a note with links back, or drag one into a note.
pages.md:
**Command palette → All highlights** lists every highlight in your vault:

- from **PDFs**, kept in `file.pdf.md` ([PDF reader](/workspace/pdf-reader/)),
- from **EPUB books**, kept in `book.epub.md` ([EPUB reader](/workspace/epub-reader/)),
- from **clipped pages**: passages marked `==like this==` in a note that was
  clipped from the web, or marked in [reading mode](/workspace/epub-reader/#reading-mode-for-clipped-pages).

## Find

Type in the search box to search the highlighted text, its note and its tags.
Case, spacing and Hebrew niqqud don't matter. Narrow the list by **kind**
(PDF, EPUB, clips), by **document** and by **tag**. Click a highlight to
open it: the reader opens at its page or chapter and flashes it.

## Tags

Type a tag under a PDF or EPUB highlight and press Enter. The tag is saved
with the highlight in its note (`file.pdf.md` or `book.epub.md`), as a W3C
Web Annotation tag, so it syncs with the note. **×** removes it. A clip's
highlights show the clip's own `tags:` from its front matter.

## Export and drag

**Export to a note** writes the current list to a new note,
`Highlights <date>.md`: a section per document, each highlight as a quote with
its note, its tags and a link that opens it again.

Drag a highlight into a note or a canvas: it drops as a quote with that link.

pages.title: Import from other apps
pages.description: Bring notes from Obsidian, Notion, Evernote, Bear, Apple Notes, Google Keep, Logseq or OneNote — into a new folder, with a report, undone in one click.
pages.md:
**File → Import notes from another app…** (or the command palette) opens
the import wizard. It never touches what you already have: everything goes
into a new folder, `Imported/<name of the export>`, numbered when the name
is taken. One click — **Undo the import** in the wizard, or the command
**Undo the last import** later — takes it back.

## Three steps

1. **Pick the app** the notes come from. The wizard tells you how to export
   from it.
2. **Pick the export** — a file, several files, or a folder (or drop them on
   the wizard). Archives are opened, also archives inside archives (Notion
   zips its parts). If the files look like another app's export, the wizard
   says so and switches in one click.
3. **Check, then import.** Before anything is written you see how many
   notes, attachments and databases will come in, what will not and why,
   and how many internal links reach their note.

## What each app becomes

| App | Export to pick | What it becomes |
|---|---|---|
| Obsidian | the vault folder, or a .zip of it | the vault as it is; `.obsidian/` and `.trash/` are left out |
| Notion | Settings → Export → *Markdown & CSV* or *HTML*, the .zip as it came | names without Notion's ids; links follow the pages; **each database becomes a `.base` file** with the same columns, and each row a note whose properties are the row's cells (Yes/No, numbers and dates typed) |
| Evernote | `.enex` files (one per notebook) | a folder per notebook; tasks, images and files in place (`_resources/<note>/`); tags, author, source URL, created and updated as properties; links between notes as `[[wikilinks]]`; encrypted parts are left out and reported |
| Bear | a backup (`.bearbk`) or TextBundles | a note per bundle with its `assets/`; `::highlight::` → `==highlight==`, `#multi word tag#` → `#multi-word-tag`; trashed notes left out |
| Apple Notes | HTML or Markdown from an exporter app | a note per page; images inside the HTML (`data:` URIs) become files; links between pages follow |
| Google Keep | Google Takeout (Keep only), the .zip | checklists as tasks; labels as tags; colour and pin as properties; archived notes in `Archive/`; trashed notes left out |
| Logseq | the graph folder, or a .zip | page properties as frontmatter; `TODO`/`DONE` as tasks; block references `((id))` and `{{embed}}` as `[[Page#^id]]` / `![[…]]`; journals named by date (`2024-01-31`); `a___b` pages as folders |
| OneNote | pages or sections saved as *Single File Web Page* (`.mht`) | a note per page, its images and attached files next to it |

Dates are kept as the properties `created` and `updated` (a browser cannot
set a file's own dates). Hebrew names — files, folders, tags, properties —
stay as they are; only characters a file system refuses are replaced.

## The report

The last step shows what came in, what did not and why (the app's own
settings, its trash, a second copy of a file, a format the app cannot
convert, a damaged file), notes that came with something missing (an
attachment the export does not have, an encrypted part, no dates), and links
that point at nothing. **Save the report as a note** puts it in the import's
folder (undo takes it back too).

## Undo

Undo deletes exactly what the import wrote: its folder, and `Imported/` when
the import made it. The vault is then the same, byte for byte, as before the
import. If you changed something in the folder after the import, undo moves
the folder to the trash instead, so nothing of yours is lost.

## Limits

- Apple Notes has no export of its own, and reading its database needs the
  Mac app; the wizard imports what an exporter app saved.
- OneNote's own `.one` files cannot be read; export pages or sections as
  `.mht`.
- Notion's links to a block (`#…` after a page) go to the page: the block
  ids do not survive the export.

## How it is checked

`src/__tests__/importWizard.test.ts` imports one golden export per app
(`src/__tests__/fixtures/import/exports.ts`): 0 attachments lost, at least
98 % of internal links resolved, the Notion database as a `.base` with the
same columns and rows, and an undo that gives back the same vault hash.
`e2e/import-wizard.spec.ts` runs the wizard in the browser. The golden
exports are written from each app's documented format; real exports from
the apps are the owner's check.

pages.title: Israeli time
pages.description: A Sunday–Thursday work week, the Hebrew date next to dates, and deadlines that move off Shabbat and chagim with a note saying why.
pages.md:
Lumen's calendar knows the Israeli week and the Jewish holidays (from its own
[Hebrew calendar](/workspace/hebrew-calendar/)). Nothing here rewrites a note: a moved
deadline is a suggestion shown next to the date you wrote.

## Settings

Open the calendar under the file tree and click its settings button.

| Setting | Default | |
|---|---|---|
| Work week | Sunday–Thursday when holidays are as in Israel, else Monday–Friday | In a Sunday–Thursday week Friday and Shabbat are the weekend; in a Monday–Friday week, Shabbat and Sunday. The calendar draws days off in a muted colour. |
| Hebrew dates | On for a Hebrew interface | The Hebrew date next to dates in a note's properties and in database views: `א׳ בתשרי תשפ״ז` in Hebrew, `1 Tishri 5787` otherwise. |
| A deadline on Shabbat or a chag | Suggest the next working day | Or the previous working day, or don't move it (only say why). |

The calendar starts the week on Sunday for Hebrew (and English), and on Monday for
French, German and Russian, as each language's own calendar does.

## Which days are off

- **Shabbat**, and the weekend of your work week.
- **Every yom tov:** Rosh Hashana (two days), Yom Kippur, the first day of Sukkot, Shemini
  Atzeret, the first and seventh days of Pesach and Shavuot. In the diaspora, the second
  days too. These are the Jewish rest days of the Hours of Work and Rest Law, 1951 (§18A).
- **Yom HaAtzmaut**, in Israel: a statutory holiday (Independence Day Law, 1949), on the
  day the government rules set (moved off Friday, Shabbat and Monday).

These days are working days, but get a note: **erev chag** (often a short day),
**Chol HaMoed** (many offices close), **fasts** (Tzom Gedaliah, 17 Tammuz, Tisha B'Av…),
**Yom HaZikaron** and **Yom HaShoah**.

## Deadlines

A **deadline** is a property named `due`, `deadline`, `due_date`, `יעד`, `תאריך יעד`,
`דדליין` or `מועד אחרון`. If it falls on a day off, you get a note:

> due: 2026-09-12 (א׳ בתשרי תשפ״ז) ⚠ Falls on Shabbat · Rosh Hashana I: suggested 2026-09-14 (Tzom Gedaliah)

Moving to the **next** working day is how Israeli law counts a period whose last day is a
day of rest (Interpretation Law, 1981, §10). Choose **previous** if you'd rather finish
before the chag.

### In a database view

Name the deadline column in the `database` block:

````md
```database
source: projects/
view: table
fields: [status, due]
deadline: due        # moved off Shabbat / chag, working days left
hebrewDate: true     # optional: overrides the setting for this block
```
````

The deadline column shows the date, the Hebrew date, the suggested working day when it
moves, and **working days left** (or overdue), counted over your work week and the
holidays. In the **calendar** view, every day has its Hebrew date and holidays, and each
item whose deadline is a day off has the suggestion under it.

## Checked

`src/__tests__/israeliTime.test.ts` has 30 golden deadlines from 2026 to 2028: every chag
on a weekday and on Shabbat, erev chag, Chol HaMoed, Yom HaAtzmaut's moves, the previous
working day, the diaspora's second days and a Monday–Friday week. Each Hebrew date is
checked against the browser's own Hebrew calendar (ICU) as well as Lumen's.

pages.title: Jewish sources from Sefaria
pages.description: Quote a verse, a mishnah or a Talmud folio by its reference, with each text's licence. Keep a copy for offline use, and see every note that cites the same verse.
pages.md:
Type a reference the way you write it, such as `בראשית א:א`, `ב״ר א, א`,
`שמות כ׳ ג׳`, `Gen. 1:1-3` or `ברכות ב.`. Lumen brings the text from
[Sefaria](https://www.sefaria.org), the open library of Jewish texts, with
its niqqud and cantillation as they are.

## Quote a source

1. Select the reference in the source editor, or put the cursor on its line.
2. Open the command palette (⌘K) and run **Insert a source from Sefaria…**.
   With nothing selected, Lumen asks for the reference.
3. **Confirm the lookup.** The question says exactly what is sent: only the
   reference (for example `Genesis 1:1`), nothing from your notes.

The quote replaces the reference:

```markdown
> **[[Genesis.1.1|בראשית א׳:א׳]]**
>
> בְּרֵאשִׁ֖ית בָּרָ֣א אֱלֹהִ֑ים …
>
> — [Sefaria](https://www.sefaria.org/Genesis.1.1) · עברית: Miqra according to the Masorah ([CC-BY-SA](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/)) · English: … (CC-BY-NC) — link only
```

Every version's title and licence are written next to it. The link
`[[Genesis.1.1|…]]` makes the verse a node in the graph.

## Licences: what is copied and what is only linked

Sefaria gives each version of a text, in each language, its own licence.
Lumen reads that licence from Sefaria's own data and follows it:

| Licence | In your note | In the offline copy |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Public Domain, CC0 | the text | the text |
| CC-BY, CC-BY-SA | the text, with its credit and licence | the text, with its credit and licence |
| CC-BY-NC, CC-BY-NC-SA, CC-BY-NC-ND | a link only | not stored |
| Copyright, or no licence noted | a link only | not stored |

**Non-commercial licences count as not free.** A note travels: it syncs,
gets published and gets exported, and Lumen cannot know what it will be used
for. **"No licence noted" means Sefaria has not checked the copyright yet.**
A non-free text is dropped as soon as Sefaria's answer is read. It never
reaches a note, the vault or a cache.

## Keep a copy for offline use

Saving is your choice and never automatic. Use the **Save for offline**
button on the message after a quote, or run **Save this source for offline**.
The copy goes to `Sources/Sefaria/.md`:

- **its frontmatter** records every version's title, licence, licence link and
  source, and whether it was copied;
- **its body** holds the free texts only.

Once a source is saved, quoting it again uses the copy: no request, no
question, and it works with no network at all.

## My notes on this verse

Put the cursor on a reference, or open a saved source note, and run **My notes
on this verse**. Lumen lists every note that cites the verse, through a wiki
link (`[[בראשית א:א]]`, `[[Genesis.1.1]]`) or a Sefaria link. The search
reads your vault on this device and sends nothing.

## Privacy

A lookup sends only the reference to `www.sefaria.org`. The privacy ledger
lists each lookup as a consented request, and the cloud-routes table lists it
as `sefaria-texts`. The *local only* policy doesn't block a lookup you
confirmed, the same way it treats a diagram you chose to send.

## What is recognised

- **Books:**
  - the Tanakh, with Hebrew and English names and the usual abbreviations
    (`בר׳`, `ש״א`, `Gen.`, `1 Sam`);
  - Midrash Rabbah (`ב״ר`, `שמו״ר` …);
  - the Mishnah (`משנה ברכות א:א`, `אבות א:א`);
  - the Babylonian Talmud (`ברכות ב.`, `ב״מ נט:`, `Berakhot 2a`).
- **Numbers** can be Hebrew numerals, with or without geresh or gershayim
  (`קי״ט`, `טו`), or digits. A range is written `א:א-ג`.
- **Not supported yet:** commentaries (`רש״י על בראשית א:א`), the Jerusalem
  Talmud, halakhic codes, and ranges that cross chapters.

## About Sefaria

Lumen uses Sefaria's public texts API, which needs no key. "Sefaria" is a
trademark of Sefaria; Lumen is not made or endorsed by Sefaria.

pages.title: JSON Canvas (Obsidian .canvas)
pages.description: Open Obsidian canvases in Lumen's Excalidraw canvas and write them back as .canvas files. JSON Canvas is an open, MIT-licensed format.
pages.md:
[JSON Canvas](https://jsoncanvas.org) is the open format Obsidian uses for its
canvases (`.canvas` files, spec 1.0, MIT licensed). Lumen's
[canvas](/workspace/canvas/) reads and writes it. Everything runs on your device.

## Import

- **Import .canvas** in the canvas bar: pick a `.canvas` file. It becomes a new
  canvas, `canvases/<name>.excalidraw`, and opens. If that name is taken, you
  get `<name>-2`, `<name>-3` and so on, and nothing is overwritten.
- A `.canvas` file already in the vault's `canvases/` folder (for example from
  a synced Obsidian vault) is listed in the picker with a **Convert** button,
  like old tldraw canvases. The `.canvas` file stays as it was.

## Export

**Export .canvas** writes the open canvas to `canvases/<name>.canvas`, next to
its `.excalidraw` file, byte for byte in Obsidian's own layout (tabs, one
node or edge per line, no space after a colon). A canvas from Obsidian that
you import and export without edits comes back byte-identical.
Exporting again replaces that `.canvas` file. The `.excalidraw` file is not
touched.

## How it maps

| JSON Canvas | Excalidraw |
|---|---|
| Text node (Markdown) | Rectangle with the text inside (shown as written, not rendered) |
| File node (`file`, `subpath`) | Rectangle showing the path, with the path as the element's link |
| Link node (`url`) | Rectangle showing the URL, with the URL as the element's link |
| Group (`label`) | Frame with the label as its name. Nodes inside it belong to the frame (to the smallest one, since Excalidraw frames don't nest) |
| Edge (`fromSide`/`toSide`, `fromEnd`/`toEnd`, `label`) | Arrow bound to both nodes at those sides, with arrowheads per end and the label on the arrow |
| Colour: preset `1`–`6` or hex | Stroke colour (the presets as Obsidian draws them: red, orange, yellow, green, cyan, purple) |

**Round trip.** Each element keeps the node or edge it came from, so a canvas
that is imported and exported without edits comes back the same, including
what Excalidraw has no place for: a file's subpath, a group's background, and
fields added by other apps. Edits are written back. Moved or resized nodes,
changed text, a changed link (`Notes/Plan.md#Goals` → `file` + `subpath`),
recoloured elements and arrows that now connect different nodes are all
exported.

**Drawn in Excalidraw.** Rectangles, ellipses and diamonds become text nodes
(with the text inside them), a shape with a link becomes a link or file node,
free text becomes a text node, frames become groups, and arrows bound to two
of those become edges. Images, free-hand strokes, lines and arrows not
connected at both ends have no JSON Canvas form. They are left out of the
`.canvas` file, the export says how many, and they stay in the
`.excalidraw` canvas.

pages.title: Large vaults and long notes
pages.description: How Lumen stays fast with 10,000 notes and with a single 2 MB note — and how that is measured.
pages.md:
Lumen is built to stay responsive with a vault of **10,000 notes** and with a
single note of **2 MB** (plan 8.4). Nothing needs to be switched on; this page
explains what happens and what to expect.

## A vault with thousands of notes

- **The index lives in a Web Worker.** Search (`⇧⌘F`), backlinks and the tags
  panel read one shared index of your notes. It is built once, in a
  background worker, so a query over 10,000 notes never blocks typing.
  Hebrew search (niqqud, final letters and prefix letters folded) is prepared
  when a note is indexed, not on every query.
- **A save re-indexes only that note.** After the first build, saving a note
  re-reads that note alone; renaming or deleting a note or a folder moves or
  drops its entries without reading anything. When files change behind
  Lumen's back (another tab, a folder edited elsewhere), the index re-lists
  the vault and re-reads only the files whose modification time changed.
- **The file tree and the index share one listing** of the vault after a
  structural change.
- **Big vaults open with folders collapsed.** With more than 1,000 notes the
  file tree starts with its folders closed (the folders of the open note stay
  open), so opening the vault does not render 10,000 rows.

## A very long note

From 50,000 characters on, three things change — the result on screen is the
same:

- **The outline** re-parses only the blocks that changed (a paragraph, a list,
  a code block). Opening or closing a code fence, or changing a reference
  definition (`[label]: url`), re-parses what it affects.
- **The preview** is rendered block by block. After an edit only the changed
  blocks are rendered again, and rendering pauses every few milliseconds so
  the editor stays fluid. A note with footnotes, reference definitions or
  suggestions (CriticMarkup) is rendered in one pass, as before.
- **The word count** in the status bar, and keeping a copy of the open note
  in the browser's storage for the next session, happen when you pause
  typing rather than on every keystroke.

## Targets and how they are checked

| What | Target | Checked by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Open the app with 10,000 notes | < 1 s | `e2e/perf-vault.spec.ts` (production build) |
| Save → index updated | < 50 ms | `e2e/perf-vault.spec.ts`, `src/__tests__/vaultWorker.test.ts` |
| Search 10,000 notes | < 100 ms | `e2e/perf-vault.spec.ts`, `src/__tests__/vaultWorker.test.ts` |
| Typing in a 2 MB note | < 16 ms per keystroke | `e2e/perf-vault.spec.ts` (`@nightly`) |

The unit tests count work rather than time it: a save reads one note and
re-indexes one note, a rename reads none, backlinks read only the linking
notes, a keystroke in a long note re-parses one block. The outline is
compared with the one-pass outline on random documents and random edits.

The 2 MB typing test runs every night (`.github/workflows/nightly-perf.yml`),
not on every pull request. To run it yourself against a production build:

```sh
npm run build
npx http-server dist -p 5180 -c-1 --cors &
PLAYWRIGHT_BASE_URL=http://localhost:5180 npx playwright test --project=perf
```

Each run attaches the measured numbers to the Playwright report as `perf`
annotations.

## Responsiveness budget

Load time is measured by Lighthouse; how fast each action answers is
measured separately (plan W1.22), in Chromium with the CPU slowed 4×, like a
mid-range phone:

| What | Budget |
| --- | --- |
| INP over 20 fixed interactions (palette, view modes, opening and switching notes, typing, a task checkbox, search, undo) | p75 < 100 ms |
| Key press → next frame, end of a 50 KB note | p95 < 16 ms |
| Key press → next frame, end of a 2 MB note | p95 < 33 ms |

```sh
npm run perf:inp          # measures (e2e/inp-budget.spec.ts), then gates
npm run perf:inp:gate -- --record   # also appends the run to reports/perf/inp-trend.jsonl
```

The run writes `reports/perf/inp-latest.json`. The gate compares it with
`reports/perf/inp-baseline.json` and fails when any of the three numbers is
10 % or more slower; the first run becomes the baseline
(`npm run perf:inp:gate -- --update` replaces it on purpose).

## For developers

- `src/storage/vaultIndexCore.ts` — the index (pure, runs in the worker or in
  the page); `src/storage/vaultIndex.worker.ts` and
  `src/storage/vaultIndexProtocol.ts` — the worker and its messages;
  `src/storage/workspaceIndex.ts` — the main-thread side, fed by the
  VaultBackend's events (`watchVault`).
- `src/renderer/blocks.ts` — top-level blocks of a document, re-scanned only
  around an edit; `src/renderer/incrementalToc.ts` and
  `src/renderer/incrementalPreview.ts` build on it.
- Semantic-search vectors are kept as one `Float32Array` per note, with the
  norms precomputed (`packVectors` in `src/ai/semanticSearch.ts`).

pages.title: Literature review matrix
pages.description: One table of every PDF in the vault, with question, method, sample, findings and limitations, and each value backed by a quote verified on its page. Runs on this device.
pages.md:
`⌘K` → **Literature review from the vault's PDFs** reads every PDF in the
vault on this device. Scanned pages are read with OCR. It writes:

- **one note per paper** in `Literature review/`, with five fields as
  properties: question, method, sample, findings and limitations. Under each
  value are the quotes it came from, each with a link to its page and line;
- **`Literature review.base`**, which shows the notes as a table, one row per
  paper and one column per field (Obsidian Bases format). It has two views:
  **All papers** and **Verified only**, which lists only the papers where
  every field is verified.

## No value without a quote

For each field, the passages that search finds go to the local model. The
model answers with quotes copied from those passages. Each quote is then
looked up in its passage and located on its page:

- A value is kept only when at least one of its quotes is found.
- Quotes that were made up, or that cite the wrong passage, are dropped. If
  none is left, the field shows "No value with a verified quote" instead of
  a guess.

The model is the local one in AI settings (Ollama or the browser model). A
cloud model is used only if your AI policy allows it.

## How it is measured

`eval/probes/lit-review.json` has five short papers (English and Hebrew).
For each field it records the right page and a phrase from it.

- `src/__tests__/litReview.test.ts` runs retrieval and verification on
  them with a stand-in model. Retrieval finds the right passage for 24 of
  the 25 fields, and every kept citation is on the right page. It also
  checks that a model that makes quotes up has nothing kept.
- `npm run eval:lit-review` runs the real model and reports the share of
  fields that are right.
- The acceptance set is 20 real papers, which the owner provides in the same
  file format. The plan's targets: 85% of fields right, every citation on the
  right page.

pages.title: The vault in a folder on your phone
pages.description: In the iOS and Android apps, keep the vault in a real folder — the Files app on iOS, a folder you pick on Android — and see edits made there.
pages.md:
In the phone app the vault starts in the app's private storage. **Command
palette → Move the vault to a folder…** puts it in a real folder on the
phone, where other apps can open and edit the notes:

| | Where the vault goes |
|---|---|
| **iOS** | The app's Documents folder. In the **Files** app it is *On My iPhone › Lumen*; other apps can open and edit the notes in place. |
| **Android** | A folder you pick in the system's folder picker (any folder on the phone or the SD card). Lumen keeps the permission across restarts. If the app was built without Lumen's folder plugin, the app's own folder on the device is used instead. |

The move copies every note, reads each copy back and compares it, and only
then switches; the app storage is kept as it was. **Open a folder as the
vault…** uses a folder that already has notes, without copying.

## Edits made in other apps

Lumen checks the folder every few seconds while it is open, and at once
when you come back to it (for example from the Files app). A changed note
updates in Lumen; if you changed the same note in Lumen at the same time,
you get the conflict dialog and nothing is lost (see *Changes made outside
Lumen*).

## When the folder is gone

On Android the permission can be taken back in the system settings, or the
folder can be deleted. Lumen then shows the vault as **disconnected** and
reads and writes nothing until you pick the folder again (**Reconnect**).

## Status

The app side is complete and tested against both phone file APIs. The
native pieces are listed in `mobile/README.md` in the repository: the
official `@capacitor/filesystem` plugin (iOS and the Android fallback) and
Lumen's small Android folder plugin; checks on real devices are still open.

pages.title: Obsidian Bases (.base files)
pages.description: Open, embed and edit Obsidian Bases files — what is supported, what is not, and how the golden set is checked.
pages.md:
A vault that comes from Obsidian keeps its **Bases**: `.base` files (YAML)
that turn notes into tables, cards, lists, kanban boards and maps. Lumen
reads and writes the same files, so the views survive the move both ways.

## Three ways to show a base

- **Open the `.base` file** from the workspace: the preview shows its views
  (one tab per view). The editor still shows the YAML.
- **Embed it in a note**: `![[Books.base]]` alone on a line, or
  `![[Books.base#Favourites]]` for one view.
- **Write it inline** in a fenced block:

````markdown
```base
filters:
  and:
    - file.hasTag("book")
    - 'status != "read"'
formulas:
  hours: (pages / 50).round(1)
views:
  - type: table
    name: To read
    order: [file.name, note.author, formula.hours]
    sort:
      - property: formula.hours
        direction: ASC
```
````

## What is supported

| Part of the file | Supported |
|---|---|
| `filters:` — a statement, or nested `and:` / `or:` / `not:` lists | yes (`not:` matches when none of its items match) |
| `formulas:` — computed properties, `formula.<name>`, a formula may use another | yes (a formula that refers to itself is reported) |
| `properties:` — `displayName` for column headers | yes |
| `summaries:` — your own summary formulas over `values` | yes |
| `views:` — `type`, `name`, `filters`, `order`, `sort`, `groupBy`, `limit`, `summaries` | yes |
| View types `table`, `cards` (`image:`), `list`, `kanban` (by `groupBy`), `map` (`coordinates:`) | yes |
| Plugin view types | shown as a table |
| Built-in summaries Average, Min, Max, Sum, Range, Median, Stddev, Earliest, Latest, Checked, Unchecked, Empty, Filled, Unique | yes |
| `this` — the `.base` file when opened, the embedding note when embedded | yes |

Expressions use the Bases language: `note.x` (or just `x`), `file.x`,
`formula.x`, `this.file.x`; operators `+ - * / %`, `== != < <= > >=`,
`! && ||`; text, numbers, lists `[a, b]`, regular expressions `/a.c/i`;
date arithmetic with durations (`today() - "1w"`, `date(note.due) + "1M"`).

**Functions:** 66 of the 68 functions in the Bases reference run (97 %):
all global functions except `icon()`, and every method on any value, text,
numbers, dates, lists (including `map`, `filter`, `reduce` with `value`,
`index`, `acc`), links, files, objects and regular expressions.

Not supported, with a clear message instead of a wrong value:

- `icon()` — the error reads "Bases function icon() is not supported here yet".
  Obsidian's icon set is too large to load in a note.
- `html()` — shown as plain text, never as markup (counted as not supported).

## Differences to know

- **Dates are UTC.** `today()` is the UTC date, as in database formulas, so a
  base gives the same answer on every machine.
- **`file.name` includes the extension** (`Dune.md`), as in Obsidian;
  `file.basename` is `Dune`.
- **`file.ctime`** is the modification time: the browser's file storage does
  not keep a creation time.
- **Text order** is natural (`2` before `10`), Latin before Hebrew.

## Sorting and saving

Click a column header to sort (again to reverse). For an embedded base,
**Save this sort to …** writes the new `sort:` into that view of the `.base`
file — comments, key order and everything else in the file stay as they
were. Opening and saving a base without edits keeps the same YAML data.

## Golden set

`src/__tests__/fixtures/bases/` holds 20 `.base` files and the vault they
run over (`vault.ts`). `expected.json` lists, for each file, the rows and
their order, and some values, worked out by hand from the Bases rules. The
test `basesGolden.test.ts` checks all 20, and that each file read and
written back unedited holds the same YAML.

To confirm against Obsidian 1.14: create the notes of `vault.ts` in an empty
vault, copy the 20 `.base` files into it, open each one and compare its
first view with `expected.json`. Any difference is a bug to file.

## Relations and rollups (Lumen)

Two top-level keys add Notion-style relations and rollups. They are a Lumen
extension: the file stays valid YAML, but Obsidian does not read these keys,
so their columns are empty there.

```yaml
relations:
  tasks:                 # notes whose `project` property links here
    property: project
    incoming: true
  team: members          # the notes this note's `members` links point to
rollups:
  hours:    { relation: tasks, property: estimate, function: sum }
  open:     { relation: tasks, function: count }
  next_due: { relation: tasks, property: due, function: earliest }
  cost:     { relation: team, property: rate, function: sum }
views:
  - type: table
    name: Projects
    order: [file.name, relation.tasks, rollup.hours, rollup.next_due]
```

- A **relation** follows a link property: one `[[link]]` or a list of
  them, as Obsidian writes them (aliases and paths resolve like any link).
  Outgoing by default: the notes the property points to. With
  `incoming: true` it runs the other way: the notes whose property points
  at this one. That gives you both sides of a link without writing it twice.
- A **rollup** computes `count`, `sum`, `avg`, `min`, `max`, `earliest` or
  `latest` over a property of the related notes. That can be `note.x`,
  `file.x`, one of the base's formulas (`formula.x`, computed for each
  related note), or another rollup.
- In a view, the columns are `relation.<name>` and `rollup.<name>`.
  Their headers are the names, unless `properties:` gives them a
  `displayName`.

## Calendar and timeline views (Lumen)

```yaml
views:
  - type: calendar
    name: Due
    date: due            # default: date
  - type: timeline
    name: Phases
    date: start
    end: finish          # optional: without it an item is one day long
```

- **Calendar** shows a month with each note on the day of its date.
  **Timeline** shows a bar from the start date to the end date for each note.
- To move a note to another day, drag it, or focus it and press
  **Alt + ←/→** for a day, **Alt + ↑/↓** for a week (the arrows follow the
  text direction, so in Hebrew → moves back). Only that date property changes in the note's file; every other byte
  stays as it was. A timeline bar keeps its length, so its end moves by
  the same number of days.
- In Obsidian these view types show as a table.

## Big bases and CSV

- A table of more than 200 rows draws only the rows in sight, so 10,000
  rows scroll smoothly. Filtering and sorting 10,000 notes takes well under
  100 ms.
- **Export CSV** saves the current view: its columns and rows, UTF-8 with a
  BOM, so Excel opens Hebrew correctly.
- **Import CSV…** adds one note per row to a folder named after the base:
  - The first column is the note's name.
  - The other columns become properties: numbers, `true` / `false` and
    text, with Hebrew headers kept.
  - Properties the base's filter pins (such as `type == "task"`) are added,
    so the new notes show in the view.
  - A name that's taken gets a number.

## Real vaults

The golden set was written from the Bases documentation. To check Lumen
against files people really write, `src/__tests__/fixtures/obsidian-corpus/`
holds byte-for-byte copies of seven public vaults with open licences (MIT,
and MIT + CC BY 4.0), each pinned to a commit in `manifest.json` with its
licence and a SHA-256 per file: 333 notes, 44 `.base` files and a canvas,
with callouts, `%%` comments, embeds, block ids, frontmatter and Dataview
inline fields. `node scripts/obsidian-corpus.mjs` checks the copies;
`--fetch` downloads them again. The test `obsidianCorpus.test.ts` runs
Lumen's own open → save path over every file:

- **Open and save, no edit:** every note and every `.base` comes back
  byte-identical — also when the note was saved by Windows (a byte-order
  mark and CRLF line endings stay; before W4.30 the first edit turned every
  line ending into LF and opening dropped the mark).
- **Properties:** writing a value that is already there changes nothing,
  for every editable property. A key written twice (`tags:` twice is common)
  is shown but not editable: a write could reach only one of the two.
- **Bases:** all 89 views run over their own vault without an error. The
  syntax of the first Bases releases is read too: `sort: - column: x`,
  top-level `display:`, `not()` and `empty()`, and an empty formula.
- **Rename and rename back:** the linking notes come back byte-identical; a
  `./` prefix, a `.md` in a wiki link and a Hebrew file name in a Markdown
  link are kept as written. The one exception is a link written in another
  case (`[[evergreen]]` comes back as `[[Evergreen]]`), which Obsidian
  rewrites the same way.

The WYSIWYG editor writes the note's body again on the first edit (its
Markdown writer has its own spelling of lists and emphasis); edit notes from
another app in the source editor.

pages.title: Side panels
pages.description: The file tree, outline, backlinks, tags, comments, trash and version history — what each side panel shows and how to use it.
pages.md:
Each panel has a **?** button that opens this help at its own section.

## File tree

The left sidebar lists the notes and folders of your vault. Click a note
to open it. Each note and folder has rename and delete, and folders can
take a new note or subfolder. Select several notes to move or delete them
together; a deleted note goes to the trash, and **Undo** brings it back. In
a large vault the folders start collapsed. The sidebar's edge resizes it:
drag it, or focus it and use ← and →.

## Outline

The headings of the open note, as a tree. Click one to jump there. The
outline follows the note as you type.

## Backlinks

Every note that links to the open one with a `[[wiki-link]]`, with the
line around each link. Click a backlink to open that note.

## Tags

Every tag in the vault, from `tags:` in the frontmatter and from `#tags`
in the text, with how many notes use it. Click a tag to filter the file
tree by it.

## Comments

Comments on the shared note, when you collaborate. Each card shows the
author, the text it is anchored to and the replies. Click a card to select
that text; resolve, reply to or delete a comment from its card. Show all
comments or only the unresolved ones.

## Trash

What you deleted in the last 30 days. **Restore** puts a note back where
it was; **Delete forever** removes it now. After 30 days notes are removed
for good.

## Version history

Every kept version of the open note, newest first. A version is kept every
couple of minutes while you type, on every save and when you close the
tab. Pick a version to preview it, with how much it differs from the
current text, and **Restore this version** if you want it back.

pages.title: Ask a PDF
pages.description: Questions about a PDF answered on this device from its own pages — every answer with quotes you can open at their page and line.
pages.md:
In the [PDF reader](/workspace/pdf-reader/), **Ask** opens a question box
beside the pages. The answer comes from the PDF's own text, on this
device, and every claim carries a quote with its **page and line**; a click
on a quote opens that page and marks the words.

## How an answer is made

1. **Text.** pdf.js reads the text of each page. A page without a text
   layer — a scan — is rendered and read by the on-device OCR (Tesseract,
   Hebrew and English).
2. **Passages.** The pages are cut into passages of whole lines (about 150
   words), each knowing its page and lines. They are ranked for the
   question with BM25 (Hebrew-aware: no niqqud, one-letter prefixes such as
   ו־ה־ב־ל peeled) and, when an Ollama on this machine has an embedding
   model, with embeddings too, the two rankings fused. The index is kept
   while the PDF is unchanged.
3. **Answer.** The six best passages go, numbered, to the `pdf-answerer`
   agent — through the agent runtime, so on a local model (Ollama, or the
   in-browser model) under the *local only* policy. It answers in the
   language of the question and quotes the passages word for word.
4. **Check.** A quote counts only when it is in the passage it names (or
   covers at least 85 % of it, the rule the research citations use); it is
   then placed on its page and line. An answer without one checked quote is
   sent back to the model once with the reason; quotes that still don't
   check out are left out, and the panel says how many.

If the passages don't hold the answer, the panel says *"This PDF doesn't
seem to answer that."* instead of guessing.

## Measuring it

`npm run eval:pdf-chat` asks the questions of the PDF golden set (plan
7.10, `eval/golden/pdf-qa`) against your Ollama and reports the share of
answers whose checked quote is on the page that holds the answer (target:
≥ 85 %). `LUMEN_EVAL_MODEL` picks the model; `LUMEN_EVAL_PDF_DIRS` adds the
held-out test split built with the golden seed. The normal test run checks
the retrieval on the same PDFs without a model.

pages.title: PDF reader and highlights
pages.description: Read PDFs in the vault, highlight text (Hebrew included), and keep every highlight as a W3C Web Annotation in a Markdown note that links back to the page.
pages.md:
Lumen opens a PDF from your vault in a reader of its own. You can select
text on a page and highlight it, add a note to a highlight, and search the
whole document. Every highlight is saved in an ordinary Markdown note next
to the PDF, with a link that opens the PDF at that page and flashes the
highlight.

Everything happens on your device. The PDF is never uploaded.

## Open a PDF

- **Command palette** (⌘K / Ctrl+K) → **Open a PDF for reading…** copies a
  PDF from your computer into the vault and opens it.
- **File tree**: click a `.pdf` file in the vault.
- **A link** in any note: `[[paper.pdf]]`, or `[[paper.pdf#page=3]]` to
  open it at page 3.

Pages are rendered only when they come near the screen, so long documents
open quickly. Use **−** / **+** / **Fit width** to zoom, and type a number
in the page box to jump to a page.

## Highlight text

1. Select text on a page.
2. Press **Highlight**, or the **H** key.

The highlight appears over the words and in the **Highlights** list on the
side. Write in the box under a highlight to add a note; it is saved when
you leave the box. **Delete** removes the highlight.

Highlights work the same in right-to-left text: select Hebrew words and the
highlight covers exactly those words on the line.

## The highlights note

The highlights of `paper.pdf` are kept in `paper.pdf.md`, in the same
folder. **Open the notes** in the reader opens it. It holds a readable list:

```markdown
- [[paper.pdf#page=3&highlight=1a2b3c4d|p. 3]] “the sentence you highlighted” — your note
```

Click a link in the preview and the reader opens at that page and flashes
the highlight.

Below the list there is a fenced `json lumen-pdf-annotations` block with
the highlights as [W3C Web Annotations](https://www.w3.org/TR/annotation-model/):
a `FragmentSelector` for the page (`page=3`, in the
[RFC 3778](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3778) form PDF links use),
refined by a `TextQuoteSelector` (the exact text, with a little of the text
before and after it) and a `TextPositionSelector`. Other annotation tools
can read them.

Lumen only rewrites the part of the note between the
`lumen:pdf-annotations` markers. Anything you write above or below them is
kept.

### When the PDF's text changes

A highlight is found again by its quote, not by its position. If the text
on the page moved, was split into lines differently, or a few characters
changed (a re-saved file, a newer PDF engine), the highlight still lands on
the right words. If the text is gone, the highlight stays in the list with
a note that its text wasn't found.

## Search

Type in **Search in this PDF** and press Enter; Enter again goes to the
next match, Shift+Enter to the previous one. Search ignores case, extra
spaces and Hebrew vowel marks (niqqud). ⌘F / Ctrl+F jumps to the search box
while the reader is open, and Esc closes the reader.

## Scanned pages

A page that is only an image has no text to select. The reader says so and
offers **Recognise text (OCR)**: the page's text is recognised on your
device (Hebrew and English, the same OCR as image import) and shown under
the page, where you can search it and highlight it. The recognised text is
not saved with the PDF, so run OCR again to see those highlights after
reopening.

## Limits

- Highlights are made within one page; a selection that runs onto the next
  page is cut at the end of the first.
- Encrypted (password-protected) PDFs don't open.
- The PDF must be in the vault, which needs a browser with the Origin
  Private File System.

pages.title: Print and PDF
pages.description: Print a note or save it as a PDF the way a word processor would, with page numbers (Hebrew numerals too), a header and footer, a table of contents, clean page breaks and embedded fonts.
pages.md:
**Print / Save as PDF…** (in the File menu and the command palette) opens the system print dialog. Choose "Save
as PDF" to get a file. The layout is built for paper, and for Hebrew first.

## What you get

- **Direction and language from the note.** A Hebrew note prints right to
  left, even from the English interface. Because the language is set
  correctly, the PDF's text can be searched and copied.
- **Header:** the note's title on every page except the first.
- **Footer:** "page / pages", as `1 / 5` or in Hebrew numerals `א / ה`.
- **Clean page breaks.** A heading never sits alone at the bottom of a page.
  Tables, rows, images, code blocks, callouts and display math are never
  split. A long table repeats its header row on every page.
- **Forced breaks:** a paragraph that is just `\newpage` or `\pagebreak`.
- **Embedded fonts.** The app's own OFL fonts (Heebo and Frank Ruhl Libre
  for Hebrew, Inter and Source Serif 4 for Latin) are embedded in the PDF,
  so it looks the same on any computer.
- **Light theme on paper,** whatever theme the screen uses.

## Settings, per note

Put these in the note's frontmatter:

```yaml
---
toc: true              # a table of contents (h1–h3) on the first page, with working links
page-numbers: hebrew   # decimal (default), hebrew or none
header: Quarterly memo # header text; "" for none
footer: Confidential   # text before the page number
page-size: Letter      # A4 (default) or Letter
---
```

## On a phone or tablet

The same command works in mobile browsers and in the installed app. When the
browser blocks the print window, as installed apps and iOS do, Lumen prints
from the current page instead.

## Limits

- **Footnotes print at the end of the note,** not at the bottom of each
  page. Chromium's print engine has no per-page footnotes.
- **The table of contents has no page numbers.** Its entries are links,
  which still work in the PDF.
- **Copying from the PDF:** Hebrew and English words copy in reading order.
  A number with a punctuation mark right next to it inside Hebrew text
  (`1:`) can come out of some PDF readers swapped (`:1`). This happens in the
  PDF's text layer, not in what is printed.

## Tested

Ten golden notes are printed on every test run: a Hebrew report, a long
table, a table of contents, footnotes, callouts, code and math, images,
page breaks, an English Letter memo and nested lists. Each is compared with
an approved image (under 1% of pixels may differ). Each PDF's text is also
read back with `pdftotext` to check the reading order, the page numbers and
the embedded fonts.

pages.md:
**⌘K → Properties: edit this note's frontmatter** opens a side panel with the
YAML front matter of the open note, one row per key.

## Field types

Each key gets a field that fits its value: **text**, **number**, **date**,
**list**, **checkbox** or **link** (`[[Note]]`). Pick a different type from the
row's menu. A link opens its note, and says so when no note has that name yet.
Values that other notes already use for the same key are offered as you type.

## Adding and removing

At the bottom, type a property name, pick its type and press **Add property**.
A name that already exists is refused, with its name. The **×** on a row
removes that key.

## What changes in the file

Only the value you edited. Comments, the order of keys, quoting and line
endings stay as they were, so the note's history shows one small change. A
value the panel can't show as a field (a nested map, for example) is
read-only here: edit it in the editor.

When the front matter isn't valid YAML, the panel doesn't guess. It says so,
and you fix it in the editor.

pages.title: Quick capture (inbox)
pages.description: Add a thought, task or link to inbox.md in two steps, from the keyboard, the home screen or the share sheet.
pages.md:
Quick capture adds one entry to the end of `inbox.md`, at the root of
your workspace. It takes two steps: open the capture box, type and press
Enter. You stay in the note you were working on. (Sharing is the
exception: it opens the inbox afterwards.)

Each entry is a list item that links to that day's
[daily note](#how-an-entry-looks) and records the time:

```markdown
# Inbox

- [[journal/2026-10-20]] 09:05 call the plumber
- [[journal/2026-10-20]] 14:30 Shared page <https://example.com/a>
  the text that was shared with it
```

If `inbox.md` doesn't exist, the first capture creates it with an
`# Inbox` heading. Quick capture only ever adds text after the last
character of the file. It never changes or reorders what is already
there. If the inbox is open in a tab with unsaved edits, the entry is
added to that open text, so your edits are kept.

Hebrew and other right-to-left text is saved exactly as you typed it,
including bidi marks. The capture box sets its direction from the first
letter you type.

## Opening the capture box

| Where | How |
|---|---|
| Any browser, the installed app, the desktop app | `⌥⌘N` (Windows / Linux: `Ctrl+Alt+N`) or **Quick capture** in the command palette (`⌘K`) |
| Installed app (PWA), home screen / dock / taskbar | Long-press or right-click the Lumen icon, then **Quick Capture**. This opens `/?capture=1`. |
| Desktop app (Tauri) | **File ▸ Quick capture…**, or `⌥⌘N` in the window |

On Windows and Linux, `Ctrl+Alt+N` is skipped when it is really AltGr+N
(which types a letter such as `ń` on some layouts).

In the box, **Enter** saves, **Shift+Enter** starts a new line and
**Esc** closes. **Open inbox** opens `inbox.md` in a tab.

## Sharing to Lumen (Android)

When Lumen is installed as an app on Android, it appears in the system
share sheet. Anything you share to it is added to the inbox as one entry:
the title and link first, then the shared text on the next line. Lumen
then opens the inbox. If this browser can't provide a workspace (no
OPFS), the shared item opens as a new note instead.

The share target uses `GET /?title=…&text=…&url=…`. Only text and links
can be shared. Sharing files would need a POST share target and a custom
service worker.

Sharing from the native iOS and Android apps (Capacitor) is a separate
feature, planned with the native apps (plan 13.3).

## How an entry looks

- `[[…]]` is the path of that day's daily note (folder and file name,
  without `.md`), built from your daily-note folder and file pattern (**Calendar ▸ Daily note settings**). If that
  note doesn't exist yet, the capture creates it from your daily-note
  template, so the link always opens it. An existing daily note is never
  changed.
- The time is your device's local time, as `HH:MM`.
- Blank lines before and after the text are removed, as are spaces at
  the ends of lines. All other lines are indented by two spaces so they
  stay inside the list item.

## A system-wide shortcut on the desktop

In a browser and the installed PWA, `⌥⌘N` works while Lumen's window has
the focus. A shortcut that works from any app needs Tauri's
global-shortcut plugin, which the desktop app doesn't bundle yet. The
frontend already checks for it at startup
(`src/capture/desktopShortcut.ts`). On macOS it registers `⌥⌘N`
(`Alt+Command+N`) when the plugin is there, and otherwise does nothing.
On Windows and Linux it registers nothing: there `Ctrl+Alt+N` is also
what many keyboard layouts send for AltGr+N, and a system-wide shortcut
can't tell them apart, so typing that letter in any app would open Lumen.
To turn it on in your own build:

1. `src-tauri/Cargo.toml`, under the desktop dependencies:
   `tauri-plugin-global-shortcut = "2"`
2. `src-tauri/src/lib.rs`, in `run()` under `#[cfg(desktop)]`:
   `app.handle().plugin(tauri_plugin_global_shortcut::Builder::new().build())?;`
3. `src-tauri/capabilities/default.json`: add
   `"global-shortcut:allow-register"` and `"global-shortcut:allow-unregister"`.

After that, on a Mac, pressing `⌥⌘N` anywhere brings Lumen to the front with the
capture box open. The window permissions this needs (`show`,
`unminimize`, `set-focus`) are already granted.

pages.title: Related notes while writing
pages.description: The notes closest to the paragraph you are writing, and the notes it mentions without a link — on this device, without slowing typing.
pages.md:
**⌘K → Related notes: show / hide** opens a small panel next to the editor.
While you write it shows:

- **Related** — up to five notes closest to the paragraph at the cursor.
  The paragraph's rarest words are searched with the workspace's BM25
  index (Hebrew prefix letters, full/defective spelling and synonyms
  included). When you built an on-device embedding index (Ollama or the
  in-browser model), its results are blended in. A cloud embedding index
  is never used here, so typing sends nothing anywhere. Click a note to
  open it.
- **Mentioned, not linked** — note names that appear in the paragraph
  without a `[[link]]`. They are underlined (dotted) in the editor. **Link**
  turns that mention into `[[Name]]` (or `[[Name|as you wrote it]]`) as one
  edit that Undo takes back. A Hebrew prefix letter stays outside the
  link. The word you are typing is left alone until you move on.

## It never gets in the way of typing

Nothing runs on a keystroke. The panel updates 100 ms after you stop
typing or move the cursor, and ranking a paragraph against 10,000 notes
takes a few milliseconds, so it is up to date well within 150 ms. Your
text changes only when you press **Link**.

## Turning it off

- For **one note**: add `related: false` to its front matter.
- For **a folder**: ⌘K → *Related notes: on / off for this folder* (for the
  folder of the open note; stored on this device).
- Everywhere: close the panel.

pages.title: Daily review (spaced repetition)
pages.description: Review your highlights and question::answer cards a few minutes a day, scheduled by FSRS, with everything kept in the vault.
pages.md:
**Command palette → Daily review** shows today's cards, 5–10 at a time. Each
one comes back just before you would forget it.

## What becomes a card

- **Highlights** from PDFs, books and clipped pages: the same ones as in
  [All highlights](/workspace/highlights/). The card shows the passage; the
  back shows its note and where it is from.
- **Question::answer lines** in any note, one per line:

  ```md
  What does FSRS stand for? :: Free Spaced Repetition Scheduler
  מה בירת צרפת? :: פריז
  ```

  The question needs a space in it or must end with a question mark, so
  Dataview-style fields such as `status:: done` are not cards. Lines in code
  blocks are skipped.

## Reviewing

Read the card and recall it. Press **space** (or the button) to see the
answer, then rate how it went: **1 Again**, **2 Hard**, **3 Good**, **4
Easy**, by key or by button. The name of the source opens the note or the
highlight. Each review has the cards that are due, most overdue first, then
up to 5 new ones a day.

## Where it is kept

The schedule of every card is in `.lumen/review.json` in your vault, so it
syncs with the vault and moves with it to another device. Editing a card's
text in its note keeps its schedule. A card whose highlight or line was
removed stays in the file, with its history, but is no longer shown.

Scheduling is FSRS-5 with its default parameters, asking for 90% recall at
each review.

pages.title: Search operators and #tags
pages.description: Narrow a search with tag:, path:, "phrases", /regex/ and -exclusions; tags written in the text count like front-matter tags.
pages.md:
The search dialog (`⇧⌘F`) and the agents' `search_workspace` tool read the
same operators. Mix them freely with ordinary words. Every operator must
hold (AND), and the words rank the notes that are left.

| Operator | Finds notes… | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `tag:name` | with this tag, in the front matter or as `#name` in the text. `tag:a` also matches nested `#a/b` | `tag:project` |
| `path:text` | whose path contains *text* (any case) | `path:daily/` |
| `"a phrase"` | that contain the phrase as written (any case; Hebrew ignores niqqud) | `"launch plan"` |
| `/regex/flags` | whose text matches the regular expression; flags `i m s u` | `/^TODO:/m` |
| `-anything` | that do **not** match it: `-tag:archive`, `-path:daily`, `-"draft"`, `-/x/`, `-word` | `tag:project -tag:archive` |

A query made only of operators lists the matching notes, newest first,
with the snippet on the match. A `/regex/` that doesn't compile returns no
notes; it never falls back to returning every note.

## Tags in the text

`#tag` anywhere in a note counts as a tag, like `tags:` in the front matter,
in the Tags panel and for `tag:`.

- Letters of any script count: `#פגישות` is a tag.
- `/` nests tags: `#meeting/standup`.
- These are **not** tags: headings (`# Title`), anything in code
  (`` `#x` `` or a fenced block), numbers such as `#42`, and URL fragments
  (`page#section`).

## How it is tested

`src/__tests__/searchOps.test.ts` runs 30 operator queries on a fixed
12-note vault (English, Hebrew, nested tags, tags in code), each checked
against the exact set of notes it must return. The queries run through the
same index the dialog uses.

pages.title: Workspace search (BM25 + Smart)
pages.description: Fast keyword search by default, semantic embeddings on demand.
pages.md:
`⌘K → Search workspace…` opens the workspace search dialog (the palette
shows `⇧⌘F` next to it, but that key toggles focus mode today). Three tabs:

## Search (BM25)

The default: keyword and filename search across every `.md` / `.txt`
note in your workspace, ranked by BM25. Agents use the same search
(`search_workspace`).

- Hebrew-aware: niqqud, final letters (ם/מ, ן/נ…) and the prefix letters
  ו ה ב כ ל מ ש are folded, so *בבית*, *והבית* and *הַבַּיִת* all find
  *בית*. The exact form you typed still ranks first.
- Full and defective spelling meet: *תכנית* finds *תוכנית*, *צהרים* finds
  *צהריים*, *ראיון* finds *ריאיון* (the exact spelling still ranks first).
- Other forms of a word count too, a little less: *אבודות* finds *אבודה*,
  *מזרחנים* finds *מזורחן* (plural, construct and possessive endings).
- A few common synonyms are searched along (*טלפון* / *סמארטפון*,
  *רכב* / *מכונית*, *פגישה* / *ישיבה*…), and common Hebrew words also
  look for their English equivalent, so *מתכון לעוגת שוקולד* finds an
  English *chocolate cake recipe* note — after the Hebrew notes.
- Question words (*מתי*, *איפה*, *למי*, *what*, *when*…) don't count, so
  you can type a question.
- A match in the note's name counts more than one in its text, and the
  whole query found as a phrase counts extra.
- The index is built on the first search and then updated one note at a
  time as you save; a 10 000-note vault answers in a few tens of
  milliseconds.
- Each hit shows a snippet with the match highlighted; the top 40 are
  listed.
- Operators narrow the search: `tag:`, `path:`, `"phrase"`, `/regex/` and
  `-` to exclude. See [Search operators and #tags](/workspace/search-operators/).

Measured by `src/__tests__/hebrewSearch.test.ts` on the probe set
`eval/probes/hebrew-search.json` (30 morphology queries, 30 full/defective
spelling pairs, 5 Hebrew→English queries) and on the HeQ dev split, which
must not drop.

## Smart (semantic)

Hybrid retrieval that fuses BM25 with cosine similarity over embedding
vectors via Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF, k = 60). The vectors come from the
first model available, local first: an Ollama embedding model
(`nomic-embed-text` or another one you installed), then the built-in
`multilingual-e5-small` in the browser (384 dimensions, about 100 languages,
Hebrew included), and OpenAI `text-embedding-3-small` only under the
*cloud* AI policy. Vectors from different models don't mix, so a change of
model rebuilds the index. Smart search finds notes that are semantically
related even when the surface words don't match — a query for
*"deep learning"* surfaces a note titled *"Neural networks"*.

To enable:

1. Switch to the **Smart** tab.
2. Click **Build index** (one-time, then incremental on subsequent runs).
3. Type your query — results re-rank in real time.

**Cost**: each chunk is embedded once and cached in IndexedDB, and
re-indexing only re-embeds chunks whose hash changed. A local model costs
nothing. With OpenAI, a 100-note workspace embeds in ≈ 8s and ≈ 200 K
tokens (≈ $0.004 with `text-embedding-3-small`).

## Cross-language: ask in Hebrew, find English sources

With the built-in embedding model (multilingual-e5-small, MIT, runs on this
device), **Smart** search finds English notes, papers and clippings for a
Hebrew question. Hebrew and English land in the same vector space, and BM25
adds its Hebrew→English word list. Each hit in another language than the
question shows a local translation under the original:

- from the local translation engine, when one is installed;
- otherwise from the browser's own on-device translator (Chrome), and only
  when the language pair is already on the device. A search never starts a
  download.
- With neither, the original is shown and the dialog says so. Nothing is
  sent anywhere.

Two limits:
- The Ollama embedding model `nomic-embed-text` is English-only. With it,
  Hebrew questions reach English notes only through keywords, and the dialog
  says so.
- On a 10,000-note vault, ranking takes about 15 ms. Embedding the question
  comes on top of that.

How it is measured:
- `eval/probes/crosslingual-he-en.json` has 50 Hebrew questions over 50
  English research abstracts, written for this repository. Its numbers are
  development numbers. On it, BM25 alone reaches nDCG@10 0.18.

sections.text: ⌘K → Search workspace… opens the workspace search dialog (the palette shows ⇧⌘F next to it, but that key toggles focus mode today). Three tabs:

sections.heading: Search (BM25)
sections.text: The default: keyword and filename search across every .md / .txt note in your workspace, ranked by BM25. Agents use the same search (search workspace). Hebrew-aware: niqqud, final letters (ם/מ, ן/נ…) and the prefix letters ו ה ב כ ל מ ש are folded, so בבית , והבית and הַבַּיִת all find בית . The exact form you typed still ranks first. Full and defective spelling meet: תכנית finds תוכנית , צהרים finds צהריים , ראיון finds ריאיון (the exact spelling still ranks first). Other forms of a word count too, a little less: אבודות finds אבודה , מזרחנים finds מזורחן (plural, construct and possessive endings). A few common synonyms are searched along ( טלפון / סמארטפון , רכב / מכונית , פגישה / ישיבה …), and common Hebrew words also look for their English equivalent, so מתכון לעוגת שוקולד finds an English chocolate cake recipe note — after the Hebrew notes.
